passages.title: Oaths by the sky, the promised Day, and the witness
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Burūj 1–3 — Three Oaths Before a Terrible Story

These three ayat are a solemn series of oaths: by the sky with its *burūj*, by the promised Day, and by a witness and that which is witnessed. They form one rising sentence of testimony before the sūrah turns, in ayah 4 onward, to the crime they answer to: the burning alive of believers by the People of the Ditch. Everything in these oaths points toward judgement, watching, and reckoning, and that is precisely what the story that follows will need.

## Why open with oaths at all?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the threads together: Allah here swears by four things — the sky with its stellar formations, the Day of Judgement, Friday, and the day of ʿArafah — and the connection between these objects of oath and what is sworn *about* is deliberate. They bear evidence to Allah's omnipotence and stand as proof of the reckoning, reward, and punishment of the Day of Judgement. The oath then serves its subject: it curses the disbelievers who burned Muslims for their faith, and gives glad news to the steadfast believers of elevated ranks in the Hereafter. In other words, these ayat are not decoration; they are the courtroom being convened.

There is also a quiet thread of *witnessing* running through the whole passage. Ayah 3 swears by "a witness and what is witnessed"; ayah 7 will describe the persecutors sitting as *witnesses* to what they did to the believers; and ayah 9 answers them: "And Allah is Witness over everything" — nothing in the heavens or the earth is concealed from Him, as Ibn Kathir explains. The tyrants watched their victims burn; Allah was watching the tyrants.

## Ayah 1 — the sky and its burūj

**What are the burūj?** The word *burūj* (singular *burj*) is opened up richly in both commentaries.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān begins with the language. A *burj* is a large mansion or fortress — the Qurʼān itself uses the word this way: "even though you are in fortified castles" (4:78). Its root sense is *to become manifest*: the related word *tabarruj* means to display one's beauty, as in the verse forbidding women "to display your beauty as it was previously displayed in the Time of Ignorance" (33:33). So a *burj* is something that stands out, towering and manifest.

As for what the burūj *are* in this verse, the sources record several views:

- **The giant stars.** This is the position Ibn Kathir adopts, and he notes it is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ad-Daḥḥāk, al-Hasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī. He connects it to Allah's words: "Blessed is He Who has placed in the heaven Burūj, and has placed therein a great lamp (the sun), and a moon giving light" (25:61). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says this is the majority view of the commentators.
- **The beautiful creation** — the reading of al-Minhāl bin ʿAmr: the oath is by the sky in its sheer beauty of construction.
- **The stations of the sun and moon.** Ibn Jarīr preferred this: twelve burūj through which the sun travels, one each month, while the moon passes through each in two and a third days — twenty-eight positions in all, with the moon hidden for two nights.
- **Mansions or castles reserved in the sky for the guardian angels**, a view other commentators mention.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a valuable caution about a later, astrological reading. Some later commentators adopted the picture of the old philosophers, in which the "fixed" stars are literally embedded in twelve zodiacal divisions of the sky. The commentary calls this absolutely incorrect: according to the Qurʼān, Allah has not fixed the stars and planets into the skies at all — "And each one is floating in an orbit" (36:40) — and the word *falak* there means not "sky" but the orbit in which each star and planet moves [Mazhari]. The oath, then, is by the real, majestic sky and its luminaries, not by the horoscope-maker's chart.

## Ayat 2–3 — the promised Day, the witness, and the witnessed

**"And by the promised Day" (ayah 2).** Ibn Kathir records from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained these very phrases: the promised Day is **the Day of Judgement**.

**"And by a witness and what is witnessed" (ayah 3).** The same hadith continues: the *witness* (shāhid) is **Friday** — "and the sun does not rise or set on a day that is better than Friday. During it there is an hour that no Muslim servant catches while asking Allah from some good except that Allah will give it to him. He does not seek refuge from any evil in it except that Allah will protect him." And the *witnessed* (mashhūd) is **the day of ʿArafah** — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies as the main day of Hajj, the 9th of Dhul-Ḥijjah. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Khuzaymah also recorded this hadith, and that it has likewise been transmitted as a statement of Abū Hurayrah himself; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the same explanation with reference to a prophetic hadith reported by Tirmidhi, rendering the two phrases as "that which attends" (Friday) and "that which is attended" (the day of ʿArafah).

**A second view.** Ibn Kathir also reports from Abū Hurayrah, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Hasan bin ʿAlī, al-Hasan al-Baṣrī, Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and ad-Daḥḥāk that the *witnessed* here is the Day of Judgement itself. Al-Baghawī, weighing the positions, said: "The majority considers the Witness to be Friday, and the Witnessed to be the day of ʿArafah."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why these two days belong in an oath about ultimate justice: Friday and the day of ʿArafah are blessed days given to the believers precisely "to accumulate treasures for the Hereafter." The very days the persecuted believers lived for are called as witnesses on their behalf.

## Where the oaths are heading

An oath this weighty demands a subject of equal weight, and it arrives immediately in ayah 4: "Cursed were the People of the Ditch." The sources tie the two halves tightly together. The persecutors — identified in Ibn Kathir's account from Muhammad bin Ishāq's Sīrah as the Yemenite king Dhū Nuwās and his army, who dug a ditch of fire at Najrān and killed believers whose only "fault" was that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, Worthy of all praise — sat by the fire as witnesses to what they were doing to the believers. The oaths deny them any illusion of impunity in advance: "Allah is Witness over everything" (ayah 9), and "those who put into trial the believing men and believing women, and then do not turn in repentance" will have "the torment of Hell, and... the punishment of the burning Fire" (ayah 10). Even here, al-Hasan al-Baṣrī marvelled at the mercy woven into the threat: "Look at this generosity and kindness. These people killed Allah's Awliya' and He still invites them to make repentance and seek forgiveness." The full story of that persecution — related in the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad and by Muslim — belongs to the ayat that follow; but it is these three oaths that frame it as a case already before the court of Allah.

## Living under these oaths

For the believer looking up at a night sky, or living through a Friday or the season of Hajj, these ayat re-charge all three with meaning. The sky's burūj bear evidence, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, to the omnipotence of the One who will convene the promised Day. Friday carries within it an hour in which no Muslim servant asks Allah for good except that He gives it to him, nor seeks refuge from evil except that He protects him — a weekly opening the Prophet ﷺ himself pointed to in explaining this very ayah. And ʿArafah, the main day of Hajj, is with Friday among the blessed days given to believers to gather "treasures for the Hereafter." To live alert to these three — the sign above, the appointment ahead, and the blessed days in between — is to live the way these oaths ask a believer to live: as someone who knows that Allah is Witness over everything, and that the promised Day will surely arrive.

passages.title: Cursed are the makers of the ditch
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the answer to the solemn oaths that opened the sūrah: a divine curse pronounced on the "People of the Ditch" — persecutors who dug trenches, filled them with blazing fire, and burned believers alive on account of their faith. What binds ayat 4–6 together is a single, terrible scene painted in three strokes: the curse upon the perpetrators (ayah 4), the instrument of their crime (ayah 5), and the chilling detail that they sat beside their own fire (ayah 6) — while the very next ayah adds that they witnessed everything they were doing to the believers.

## The words themselves

**"Qutila" (ayah 4)** — rendered "condemned" or "cursed were" — is, as Ibn Kathir explains, a declaration that the companions of the ditch stand cursed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this curse is the very subject of the oaths in ayat 1–3: Allah swears by the star-studded sky, the Promised Day, the witness and the witnessed, and then delivers this verdict against those who burned the Muslims on account of their faith — while giving cheerful news to the righteous believers of elevated ranks in the Hereafter.

**"Ukhdūd" (ayah 4)** is a trench or ditch dug in the ground; its plural, *akhādīd*, means ditches. The word matters, because the hadith of the event describes exactly this: ditches dug "at the entrances to the roads" with fires kindled in them.

**"The fire, filled with fuel" (ayah 5)** is not a passing bonfire. Ibn Kathir describes how the persecutors "lit a fire in it and prepared some fuel for it in order to keep it ablaze" — a fire deliberately stoked and maintained. This was organised, premeditated cruelty.

**"When they sat around it" (ayah 6)** is perhaps the most disturbing image in the passage. Ibn Kathir's summary of the event: a group of disbelievers went after the believers among their own people and tried to force them to abandon their religion. The believers refused to recant. So the ditch was dug, the fire lit, and they were given the choice again. They refused again — and were thrown in, while their killers *sat* by the fire. The ayah that follows this passage completes the picture: they were witnesses to what was being done to the believers.

## The story from the Sunnah

Who were these people? Imam Ahmad recorded from Suhayb — and Muslim also recorded this hadith at the end of his Sahih — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told their story at length. It deserves to be told properly, because it is one of the most extraordinary narratives of faith in the entire Sunnah.

**The boy and the two teachers.** Among the people who came before us there was a king who had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he asked the king for a boy to teach magic as his successor. A boy was sent — but on his route lay a monk, a man of true faith. The boy sat with the monk, was captivated by his words, and kept returning. Thrashed by the sorcerer for lateness and beaten at home for lateness, he followed the monk's advice to excuse himself to each by blaming the other — and kept coming.

**The test.** One day a huge, terrible creature blocked the road (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account calls it a lion) and the people could not pass. The boy said, "Today I shall know whether the sorcerer is better or the monk is better." He took a stone and said: "O Allah! If the deeds and actions of the monk are liked by You better than those of the sorcerer, then kill this creature so that the people can cross." He struck it with the stone; the creature died; the people passed. The monk, hearing of it, told him: "O my son! Today you are better than I... You will be put to trial. And in case you are put to trial, do not inform them about me."

**The healings.** The boy went on to treat congenital blindness, leprosy, and other diseases — always insisting: "I do not cure anybody; it is only Allah who cures people. So, if you believe in Allah and supplicate to Him, He will cure you." A blind courtier of the king believed, supplicated, and Allah cured him.

**The confrontation.** When the courtier returned to court seeing, the king demanded to know who had restored his sight. "My Lord," he said. "I did?" asked the king. "No — my Lord and your Lord: Allah." The king, who tolerated no Lord beside himself, tortured him until he revealed the boy; tortured the boy until he revealed the monk. The monk and the courtier were each told to abandon their religion; each refused; each was sawn in two.

**The boy Allah would not let them kill.** The boy too refused. He was taken up a mountain to be thrown from its peak — he prayed, "O Allah! Save me from them by any means that You wish," the mountain shook, his captors fell, and he walked back to the king. He was taken out to sea to be drowned — he prayed the same prayer, and his captors drowned while he returned again. Finally he told the king: "You will not be able to kill me until you do as I order you... Gather the people in one elevated place and tie me to the trunk of a tree; then take an arrow from my quiver and say: 'In the Name of Allah, the Lord of the boy.'" The king did so; the arrow struck the boy's temple; he placed his hand over the wound and died. And the plan the boy had willingly died for succeeded utterly: the assembled people proclaimed, "We believe in the Lord of the boy!"

**The ditch.** The king was told: that which you feared has taken place — by Allah, all the people have believed. So he ordered ditches dug at the entrances to the roads and fires kindled in them, and decreed: whoever abandons his religion, let him go; whoever does not, throw him into the fire. And the believers went. The hadith ends with a scene the ummah has never forgotten: a woman carrying the baby she was breastfeeding hesitated at the edge of the fire, and her baby spoke: **"Be patient mother! For verily, you are following the truth!"** (In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's wording: "O mother, be steadfast, because you are certainly on the truth.")

## Who, where, when

Ibn Kathir also relates the account of Muhammad ibn Ishaq in his book of Sīrah, which differs in some details. After the boy's murder, the people of Najran followed his religion — the religion of Christianity, which was the true religion of that era before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ. Then the king Dhū Nuwās — his name was Zurʿah, and in the time of his kingdom he was called Yusuf; his father was Tubān Asʿad Abī Karib, the Tubbaʿ who kept two rabbis with him from the Jews of Madinah, at whose hands some of the people of Yemen had accepted Judaism — came with his army and called the people of Najran to Judaism. He gave them the choice: accept Judaism or be killed. They chose death. He dug the ditch, burned some in the fire and killed others with the sword, until he had killed almost twenty thousand — in one morning. Ibn Ishaq says it was about Dhū Nuwās and his army that Allah revealed these ayat. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn ʿAbbas, identifies him as the ruler of Yemen who lived about seventy years before the birth of the Prophet ﷺ, names the martyred boy ʿAbdullah ibn Tamir, and notes reports putting the number burned at about twelve thousand or more.

Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abi Hatim, records that "trenches of fire" occurred more than once in history — one in Yemen, one in Syria, one in Iran — and that the Qur'an here refers to the first, at Najran in Yemen, because that was in Arabia.

The story has a sequel. One man, Daws Dhū Thaʿlaban, escaped the massacre on horseback and reached Caesar, the emperor of Syria, who wrote to An-Najashi, the king of Abyssinia. An army of Abyssinian Christians, led by Aryat and Abrahah, rescued Yemen; Dhū Nuwās tried to flee but fell into the sea and drowned. So the tyrant of the ditch was destroyed by the sea he had once used as an instrument of execution. Ibn Kathir closes this history by noting that he will mention a portion of it again when explaining the ayah "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the Owners of the Elephant?" (105:1).

One more remarkable report: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Muhammad ibn Ishaq that when the boy ʿAbdullah ibn Tamir's burial place had to be dug up for some important reason in the time of Sayyidna ʿUmar, his body was found intact, sitting up, hand placed over his hip joint where the arrow had struck — when the hand was moved the wound bled, and when it was replaced the bleeding stopped. On his finger was a ring inscribed *"Allah is my Lord."* The governor of Yemen informed ʿUmar, who wrote back: bury the body back as it was, with his finger-ring.

## What the passage is teaching

**The curse is Allah's own verdict.** Allah opens the sūrah with four majestic oaths and then spends them on this: *cursed were the People of the Ditch.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the oaths bear evidence to the Divine omnipotence and to the reality of reckoning, reward, and punishment on the Day of Judgement — and their subject is a curse upon the infidels who burned the Muslims on account of their faith, together with cheerful news for the righteous believers of elevated ranks in the Hereafter. By every worldly measure, the persecutors won and the believers were destroyed. By the measure of these ayat, the burned believers won elevated ranks, and the burners earned the curse of Allah, sworn to by the heaven itself.

**The fire was a choice, sustained hour by hour.** Ayah 5 does not merely mention a fire; it describes one "fed with fuel" — and Ibn Kathir spells out what that means: they lit it and prepared fuel to keep it ablaze. Ayah 6 then seats the persecutors beside it. This was not a crime of momentary rage but of settled, comfortable deliberation — men warming themselves at the instrument of their cruelty. That is precisely what the sūrah holds up for the curse.

**Steadfastness upon truth is the believer's path through persecution.** The boy's story makes the point from every side. His refrain — "I do not cure anybody; it is only Allah who cures people" — kept every miracle pointing back to Allah. He deliberately traded his single life for the faith of an entire nation, and the words "We believe in the Lord of the boy" were his triumph. And the nursing infant's sentence — "Be patient mother! For verily, you are following the truth!" — is the passage's living commentary: to stand firm upon the truth, even at the cost of everything, is victory, whatever the fire consumes.

passages.title: The believers' only crime: faith in the Almighty
passages.tafsir:
## The crime that was no crime

These three ayat sit at the heart of Surah al-Buruj's account of the People of the Ditch (Ashab al-Ukhdud) — the tyrants who dug trenches, filled them with fire, and burned believers alive for refusing to renounce their faith. What binds ayat 7–9 together is a single, devastating contrast: in ayah 7 the persecutors sit as *witnesses* to their own atrocity, in ayah 8 Allah declares that the victims' only "offence" was faith itself, and in ayah 9 the scene is turned inside out — over everything, including those men seated at the fire's edge, stands Allah, "Witness over everything." The killers watched the believers; Allah was watching the killers.

## Ayah 7: spectators at their own crime

"And they witnessed what they were doing against the believers." Ibn Kathir explains this simply: they were witnesses to what was done to these believers. Read together with the preceding ayah — "when they sat by it" — the picture is of persecutors who did not merely order the killing from a distance but seated themselves around the flames to watch. Ibn Kathir describes how it came about: a disbelieving people went after those among them who believed in Allah and tried to force them to give up their religion. The believers refused to recant, so ditches were dug in the ground, a fire was lit in them and fuel prepared to keep it ablaze; the believers were given one more chance to apostatise, refused again, and were thrown in.

The Arabic word for the watchers in ayah 7 is *shuhud* — witnesses. Hold that word; ayah 9 will return it.

## Ayah 8: "they had no fault except that they believed"

"And they had no fault except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, Worthy of all praise." Ibn Kathir's gloss: the believers had committed no sin at all in the eyes of these people — their only "crime" was faith in Allah. The verb rendered "resented" or "held against" (*naqamu*) exposes the persecutors completely: strip away every pretext, and the one thing they actually punished was belief itself.

Notice which two names of Allah the ayah chooses: **al-'Aziz** (the Almighty) and **al-Hamid** (the Worthy of all praise). Ibn Kathir draws out why. Allah is the Most Mighty — so the believers had attached themselves to One Who "does not treat unjustly those who desire to be with Him." And He is Most Praiseworthy "in all of His statements, actions, legislation, and decrees." Then Ibn Kathir confronts the hard question head-on: it was Allah, the Almighty and Praiseworthy, Who *decreed* what happened to these servants of His at the hands of the disbelievers — "even though the reason for this decree is unknown to many people." The ayah does not pretend the believers were rescued in this world. It insists instead that the One they died for is Mighty and Praiseworthy in that very decree, whether or not we can see the wisdom from where we stand.

## Ayah 9: the Witness above the witnesses

"To Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth! And Allah is Witness over everything." Ibn Kathir notes that among Allah's perfect attributes is that He is the Owner of all of the heavens, the earth, whatever is in them, and whatever is between them. And "Allah is Witness over everything" means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that nothing in the heavens or the earth is concealed or hidden from Him.

A reader of the Arabic may notice something the classical commentary before us does not itself spell out — offered here simply as an observation on the wording of the ayat: the persecutors in ayah 7 are called *shuhud*, witnesses seated around the fire, while ayah 9 declares Allah *Shahid* — Witness over everything, including them. The men at the ditch made themselves the audience of the believers' destruction; ayah 9 answers that nothing they did by that trench was hidden from the Owner of the heavens and the earth. And ayah 10 goes on to warn that those who put the believing men and women to trial and then do not repent will have the torment of Hell and the punishment of the burning Fire.

## The story behind the ayat: the boy and the king

Ibn Kathir relates the fullest account of who these believers were. Imam Ahmad recorded from Suhayb that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told the story — Muslim also recorded this hadith at the end of the Sahih — of a king in a nation before us who had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old he asked for a boy to train. On his way to the sorcerer the boy would sit with a monk, and the monk's words won his heart. When a huge creature blocked the people's road, the boy took a stone and said: "O Allah! If the deeds and actions of the monk are liked by You better than those of the sorcerer, then kill this creature so that the people can cross" — and it died. The monk told him, "Today you are better than I... You will be put to trial."

By Allah's leave the boy began to cure congenital blindness, leprosy and other diseases, always insisting: "I do not cure anybody; it is only Allah who cures." A blind courtier of the king believed, supplicated, and Allah cured him; when the king demanded to know who restored his sight, he answered: "My Lord and your Lord — Allah." The enraged king tortured him until he revealed the boy, and the boy until he revealed the monk. The monk and the courtier each refused to abandon their religion and were sawn in two. The boy was sent up a mountain to be thrown from its peak — he prayed, "O Allah! Save me from them by any means that You wish," the mountain shook, and the men who had taken him fell, while he walked back to the king. Sent out to sea to be drowned, he prayed the same prayer, and it was his escorts who drowned.

Then came the boy's astonishing choice. He told the king: you will not be able to kill me until you gather the people in one place, tie me to the trunk of a tree, take an arrow from my quiver, and say, "In the Name of Allah, the Lord of the boy." The king did exactly that; the arrow struck the boy in the temple, he placed his hand over the wound and died — and the whole crowd proclaimed, "We believe in the Lord of the boy!" The king had feared precisely this; now, told that all the people had believed, he ordered ditches dug at the entrances of the roads and fires kindled in them: whoever abandoned his religion would be let go; whoever refused would be thrown into the fire. The narration describes the people struggling and scuffling in the fire — Maʿarif ul Qurʼan records that by some reports about twelve thousand were burned, and by others more. A nursing mother hesitated at the edge — and her infant spoke: "Be patient, mother! For verily, you are following the truth!"

This is the scene the ayat memorialise: the fires, the seated spectators, and believers whose only fault was faith in the Almighty.

## Who they were: Najran and Dhu Nuwas

Ibn Kathir also relates the account of Muhammad bin Ishaq in his Sirah, which differs in some details: after the boy's death the people of Najran followed his religion — Christianity, which Maʿarif ul Qurʼan notes was the true religion of that era. Then the king Dhu Nuwas — his name was Zur'ah, called Yusuf in his kingship — came with his army and gave them a choice between Judaism and death. They chose death. He burned some in a ditch and killed others with the sword, until he had killed almost twenty thousand. Ibn Ishaq says it was about Dhu Nuwas and his army that Allah revealed these ayat to His Messenger ﷺ. One man, Daws Dhu Tha'laban, escaped on horseback; through him word reached Caesar and then the Negus (An-Najashi) of Abyssinia, whose Christian army — led by Aryat and Abrahah — rescued Yemen, while Dhu Nuwas tried to flee, fell into the sea and drowned. The tyrant's spectacle of power ended with his kingdom gone and his own death in the water.

Maʿarif ul Qurʼan adds detail: according to Ibn 'Abbas the king was Yusuf Dhu Nuwas of Yemen, living about seventy years before the birth of the Prophet ﷺ, and the boy is named as 'Abdullah Ibn Tamir. It also records, from Ibn Ishaq, that when the boy's grave was uncovered in the time of 'Umar, his body was intact, his hand placed over the spot where the arrow had struck, wearing a ring inscribed "Allah is my Lord"; 'Umar wrote back: bury the body back as it was, with his ring. Maʿarif further notes, citing Ibn Kathir from Ibn Abi Hatim, that trench-burnings happened more than once in history — in Yemen, in Syria, and in Iran — but the incident the Qurʼan refers to here is the one at Najran in Yemen, because that was in Arabia.

## Living these ayat

Two truths carry from this passage into a believer's life. First, faith may itself be the thing the world holds against you — ayah 8 says the believers of the Ditch were guilty of nothing else — and the ayah answers that charge not with rescue but with the names al-'Aziz and al-Hamid: the One you believe in is Mighty and Praiseworthy even when His decree is painful and its wisdom hidden, as Ibn Kathir says. The believers of the Ditch, the monk sawn in two, the mother at the fire's edge — none recanted, because they knew Whose they were. Second, ayah 9 is the permanent consolation of the oppressed and the permanent warning to the oppressor: every injustice has a Witness from Whom nothing in the heavens or the earth is hidden, and to Whom all dominion belongs. The Qurʼan pronounces the People of the Ditch cursed; and, as Maʿarif ul Qurʼan observes, the same passage gives glad news to the righteous believers of elevated ranks in the Hereafter.

passages.title: Recompense: torment for persecutors, Gardens for believers
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the verdict of Sūrat al-Burūj. After the sūrah has told of the People of the Ditch — the tyrants who dug trenches of fire and burned the believers alive for nothing but their faith — Allah now pronounces the two destinies: for the persecutors who never repent, the torment of Hell and the burning Fire (ayah 10); for those who believe and do righteous deeds, Gardens beneath which rivers flow, "the supreme success" (ayah 11). What binds the pair together is deliberate symmetry: the sūrah showed us fire kindled by men against the faithful, and now shows fire and Garden apportioned by Allah — each recompense answering the deed.

## "Those who put the believers to trial"

The word in ayah 10 is *fatanū* — from *fitnah*, a trial or ordeal by which a person is tested. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, and Ibn Abza all explained *fatanū* here concretely: **"they burned them."** The "trial" these tyrants inflicted was the fire pit itself — forcing believers to choose between their religion and the flames.

Notice too that the ayah names **"the believing men and the believing women"** separately. The sources' account of the Ditch makes this vivid: in the long hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Suhayb — and also recorded by Muslim at the end of his Sahih — the Prophet ﷺ told the story of the boy, the monk, and the king, ending with the people being thrown into the trenches of fire. Among the last to face it was a woman carrying her nursing baby. She hesitated at the edge — and her infant spoke: "Be patient, mother! For verily, you are following the truth!" The women who stood firm at the fire are written into the ayah alongside the men.

Ibn Kathir, drawing on Ibn Ishaq's Sirah, identifies the persecutor as Dhu Nuwas, the king of Yemen who had adopted Judaism, and who gave the Christians of Najran the choice between his religion and death. They chose death, and he burned and slaughtered nearly twenty thousand of them in a single morning.

## "And then do not repent" — the door left open

The most astonishing phrase in ayah 10 is the condition tucked into its middle: *thumma lam yatūbū* — "and then do not repent." The threat of Hell is restricted to those who **do not cease from what they are doing and do not regret what they did**, as Ibn Kathir explains. Which means the ayah is simultaneously a warning and an invitation: even these people were being called back. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the lesson out plainly: this part of the verse invites people to repent.

Al-Hasan Al-Basri captured the wonder of it in a saying quoted by Ibn Kathir and cited from him in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: **"Look at this generosity and kindness. These people killed Allah's Awliya' and He still invites them to make repentance and seek forgiveness."** The *Awliya'* of Allah are His friends, His devoted servants. They incinerated His beloved servants — and the very ayah that sentences them pauses to hold the door of tawbah (repentance) open.

## Two torments — one meaning or two?

Ayah 10 names the punishment twice: "for them is the torment of Jahannam (ʿadhāb jahannam), and for them is the torment of the burning (ʿadhāb al-ḥarīq)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings of this doubling:

**First**, the second clause may simply be explicative of the first — emphasis, stating that they will be put into Hell and suffer its eternal fire. The repetition drives the sentence home.

**Second** — and this is the more arresting possibility — the "torment of burning" may refer to a punishment **in this world**, as narrated in some reports cited by Mazhari. According to these reports, the believers cast into the pits were actually spared the agony of the fire: their souls were taken before the flames could touch them, and only their bodies lay in the furnace. Then the fire flared up so violently that it burst out of the trenches, swept through the city, and burned the very spectators who had sat watching the believers burn. Only Dhu Nuwas escaped — he fled and threw himself into the sea to save himself from the fire, and drowned. On this reading, the persecutors tasted a burning in this life and await Jahannam in the next: two torments, both named in the ayah.

Ibn Kathir states the underlying principle plainly: **"the recompense is based upon the type of deed performed."** They punished with fire, so with fire they are punished.

## Ayah 11 — the mirror image

Then the sūrah turns, with the same emphatic opening (*inna alladhīna...*, "Surely those who..."), to the other party. Ibn Kathir notes that here **Allah Himself informs about His believing servants** — the Lord who was "Witness over everything" as the believers burned now announces what He has prepared for His own.

The ayah joins two things that the Qur'an here holds together as one description: they **believe**, and they **do righteous good deeds** — faith in the heart and its proof in action. For such people, the ayah promises "Gardens under which rivers flow."

Ibn Kathir points out the deliberate contrast: this is **"the opposite of what He has prepared for His enemies of Fire and Hell."** Where the persecutors get fire upon fire, the believers get gardens and running water — flowing rivers set against trench and flame. Every element of the reward answers an element of the punishment, just as the punishment answered the crime.

## "That is the supreme success"

And Allah seals the ayah: *dhālika al-fawzu al-kabīr* — **"That is the supreme success."**

That closing phrase is the sūrah's quiet reversal of everything the story seemed to show. In worldly terms the believers of the Ditch lost everything: they were given the choice between faith and life, and they went into the fire. But the ayah names the outcome of those who believe and do righteous deeds — Gardens under which rivers flow — the *supreme success*, while the persecutors' outcome, unless they repented, is everlasting torment. Victory and defeat are redefined from the vantage of the Hereafter: the great triumph is not to walk away from the fire, but to arrive at the Gardens.

## Living it

The passage speaks first to anyone who suffers for their faith: your steadfastness is seen by Allah, Who is "Witness over everything," and the recompense He has prepared for His believing servants is Gardens and the supreme success. And it speaks, remarkably, even to the wrongdoer. The ayah itself confines the threat to those who "do not repent," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that clause as an invitation to people to repent — the same divine generosity at which al-Hasan al-Basri marvelled, extended in the very sentence that pronounces the punishment.

passages.title: The Lord's severe grip and majestic attributes
passages.tafsir:
## The severe grip, and the Names that surround it

After telling the story of the people of the trench — believers burned alive for nothing but their faith — and setting out the two destinies, Gardens beneath which rivers flow for the believers and the Fire for the enemies of Allah, the sūrah turns from the story to the One behind it. Ayat 12–16 are a portrait of the Lord Himself: His grip is severe (12), He originates and resurrects (13), He is All-Forgiving, All-Loving (14), Owner of the Throne, the Glorious (15), Doer of whatever He wills (16). What holds these five ayat together is a single argument: the promise of judgment just made is guaranteed by who Allah *is*.

## Ayah 12: "Indeed, the grip of your Lord is severe"

Ibn Kathir explains: His punishment and His vengeance upon His enemies, those who have rejected His Messengers and opposed His command, is "severe, great and strong. For verily, He is the Owner of power, Most Strong. He is the One that whatever He wants, then it will be however He wants it to be, in the matter of a blinking of an eye, or even swifter."

The sūrah has just described believers seized by fire; now it answers with a mightier seizing. Ibn Kathir notes that when the sūrah goes on to recall Firʿawn and Thamūd, that recollection is "the affirmation of His statement, 'Verily, the punishment of your Lord is severe and painful'" — for when He seizes the wrongdoer, "He seizes him with a severe and painful punishment. It is the seizing punishment of One Most Mighty, and Most Powerful." Those who persecute the believers are not, in the end, the ones doing the seizing; they are the ones who will be seized.

## Ayah 13: He originates and repeats

"He is certainly the One Who originates and resurrects." Why does this follow the severe grip? Because a persecutor's deepest assumption is that death is escape — burn the believers, and the matter is closed. Ayah 13 removes that refuge. Ibn Kathir: "from His perfect strength and power is that He begins the creation, and He repeats it just as He began it, without opposition or resistance." The One who created the first time will bring back — and no one can resist or oppose either act. The martyrs of the trench are not gone, and their killers have not gotten away with anything. Resurrection turns the grip of ayah 12 from a worldly threat into an inescapable certainty.

## Ayah 14: All-Forgiving, All-Loving — mercy in the middle of majesty

Then, astonishingly, in the very middle of this passage of power stands: "And He is the All-Forgiving (al-Ghafūr), the All-Loving (al-Wadūd)."

Ibn Kathir's comment deserves to be read slowly: "He forgives the sin of whoever repents to Him and humbles himself before Him, *no matter what the sin may be*." And on the name **al-Wadūd**, he transmits from Ibn ʿAbbās and others that it means **al-Ḥabīb — the Loving**. Allah is not merely one who pardons; He is one who loves those who turn to Him.

Severity and love are not in tension here. The same limitless power that makes His grip inescapable is what makes His forgiveness boundless: no sin is too great for the One whose power has no limit. Set between the severe grip and the irresistible will, this ayah keeps the passage from being read as bare threat — the door of repentance stands open in the very middle of it.

## Ayah 15: Owner of the Throne, the Glorious — and the two readings

"Owner of the Throne" — Ibn Kathir: "the Owner of the Mighty Throne that is above all of the creation."

Then comes a subtle beauty of the Qur'an's transmitted recitations. Ibn Kathir notes that the word **al-Majīd** ("the Glorious") has been recited in two different ways: with a *ḍammah* over its last letter (*al-Majīdu*), making it an attribute of **the Lord** — "Owner of the Throne, the Glorious One"; or with a *kasrah* under its last letter (*al-Majīdi*), making it a description of **the Throne** — "Owner of the Glorious Throne." His verdict: "both meanings are correct." Allah is Glorious, and His Throne is glorious; the two recitations together give the reader both truths at once — a richness, not a contradiction.

## Ayah 16: "Doer of whatever He wills"

The passage seals with the attribute that underwrites all the others. Ibn Kathir: "whatever He wants He does it, and there is no one who can counter His ruling. He is not asked about what He does due to His greatness, His power, His wisdom and His justice." Note the pairing — His will is unquestionable not as raw force but because it flows from greatness *and wisdom and justice* together.

Ibn Kathir relates here a moving report about Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him). During the illness of his death he was asked, "Has a doctor seen you?" He said, "Yes." They asked, "What did he say to you?" He replied: "He said, 'I am the Doer of whatever I intend.'" Abū Bakr's "doctor" was his Lord — and his answer was this very ayah. That is what it looks like when this passage has settled into a heart: at the edge of death, no panic, only surrender to the One whose decree cannot be countered and whose decree is just.

## Living this passage

These five ayat train the heart in two directions at once, and a believer needs both.

**For the wronged:** if you suffer for your faith, as the people of the trench did, these ayat are your anchor. The grip of your Lord is severe; He resurrects, so no injustice dies with its victim. Nothing is unfinished.

**For the sinner:** the same passage forbids despair. Between the severe grip and the irresistible will stands al-Ghafūr al-Wadūd — the One who, in Ibn Kathir's words, forgives whoever repents to Him and humbles himself before Him, no matter what the sin may be, and who, as Ibn ʿAbbās said of His name al-Wadūd, is the Loving toward those who return.

And for every believer, ayah 16 offers what it gave Abū Bakr: rest. The One who does whatever He wills is also the Forgiving, the Loving — the One whose doing flows from greatness, power, wisdom and justice — so what He wills for you can be met with trust.

passages.title: Destroyed tyrants past and the preserved Quran
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is doing

Sūrah al-Burūj opened with a crime: believers burned alive in a trench for nothing but their faith. The sūrah has already answered that crime with promise and warning — Gardens beneath which rivers flow for the believers, and a portrait of the Lord whose seizing is severe yet who is Oft-Forgiving and Loving. Now, in ayat 17–22, the sūrah closes by proving the warning from history and then anchoring everything in the Qur'an itself. Two movements hold these six ayat together: **the tyrants of the past were seized and could not escape** (17–20), and **the revelation the deniers reject is glorious and perfectly preserved** (21–22). The threat is real because it has already happened; the promise is reliable because its source cannot be corrupted.

## "Has the story reached you of the hosts?" (ayat 17–18)

Ayah 17 turns to the Prophet ﷺ with a question: *Has the story of the forces reached you?* — and ayah 18 names them: *Pharaoh and Thamūd*. The word rendered "forces" or "hosts" is **al-junūd**. Ibn Kathir explains the sense of the question: has the news reached you of what Allah caused to befall them of torment, how He sent down upon them a punishment **that no one was able to ward off from them?** Nothing they had could turn the seizing aside when it came.

Ibn Kathir adds that this question affirms what the sūrah has already declared about the severity of your Lord's seizing. Earlier the sūrah stated the principle; now it produces the evidence. When Allah seizes the wrongdoer, Ibn Kathir writes, He seizes him with a severe and painful punishment — "the seizing punishment of One Most Mighty, and Most Powerful." The fate of Pharaoh and Thamūd is presented not as ancient trivia but as a standing warning of what that seizing looks like when it falls.

## Denial, and the encirclement they cannot see (ayat 19–20)

Ayah 19 begins with *bal* — "Nay!" / "Yet" — a word that brushes aside what came before and corrects course. The lesson is on the table, and still: *the disbelievers persist in denial* (fī takdhīb — takdhīb being the act of calling something a lie). The Arabic phrasing pictures them as being **in** denial, immersed in it as their element. Ibn Kathir unpacks it: they are "in doubt, suspicion, disbelief and rebellion" — not honest uncertainty, but a settled, wilful rejection.

Then ayah 20 quietly closes the trap: *And Allah encompasses them* — "from behind," in Ibn Kathir's rendering, or as the translation puts it, "from all sides." While they imagine themselves free agents, mocking and denying, they are already surrounded. Ibn Kathir's comment is spare and total: Allah "has power over them, and is able to compel them. They cannot escape Him or evade Him." The deniers are not outside Allah's grasp deciding whether to enter it; they are inside it already.

## The Glorious Qur'an in the Preserved Tablet (ayat 21–22)

A second *bal* — "Nay! In fact" — pivots from the deniers to the thing they deny. *This is a Glorious Qur'an* (qur'ānun **majīd**): Ibn Kathir glosses majīd as "magnificent and noble." Their takdhīb — calling it a lie — collides with what the Book actually is: glorious, magnificent, noble.

And it is untouchable: *in a Preserved Tablet* — **al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ**, ayah 22. Ibn Kathir locates it "among the most high gathering" and explains what "preserved" (maḥfūẓ) guarantees: the Qur'an is **"guarded from any increase, decrease, distortion, or change."** Nothing can be added to it, nothing taken from it, nothing twisted in it. The deniers can mock the message and persist in takdhīb, but they cannot touch the Book itself, because its original rests where no created hand reaches.

This is a fitting last word for the whole sūrah — and with it the sūrah ends. It opened with tyrants who tried to erase faith with fire; it closes by saying, in effect, that the Word that warns them and consoles the believers is beyond the reach of every Pharaoh. Persecutors pass; the Book remains.

## Taking it to heart

For the believer under pressure, these ayat are the sūrah's final reassurance: the powers that loom largest — the "hosts" of any age — are already encompassed by the One they defy, and His warning has precedent in Pharaoh and Thamūd. For every reader, ayah 19 is a mirror to check: to be "in denial" after the evidence, in doubt, suspicion, disbelief and rebellion, is a condition to flee from, not a fate. And ayat 21–22 tell us how to hold the Qur'an in our hands: as something majīd, noble and magnificent, whose preservation Allah Himself has guaranteed — a Book worth trusting with everything, because nothing can corrupt it.
